n: Types Uses And Intravenous Fluid Therapy

faq.a: Ringer's lactate better matches plasma electrolytes and avoids hyperchloraemic acidosis; use in trauma, burns, or surgery when large volumes are needed.
faq.q: When should I use Ringer's lactate instead of normal saline?

faq.a: Current evidence shows no mortality benefit; crystalloids are first‑line, albumin reserved for refractory shock or hypoalbuminaemia.
faq.q: Is albumin superior to crystalloids for sepsis?

faq.a: Rapid rise in serum sodium can cause central pontine myelinolysis; monitor sodium every 2‑4 h and limit increase to ≤ 10 mmol/L per 24 h.
faq.q: What is the danger of giving too much 3% saline?

exam: A 25‑year‑old with severe falciparum malaria presents with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a BP of 90/60 mmHg. What is your immediate fluid plan? — Give 20 ml/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus, reassess perfusion, repeat if still hypoperfused.

You have given two 1‑L boluses of normal saline to a trauma patient; urine output falls to 0.2 ml/kg/h and lung bases develop crackles. What do you do next? — Stop fluids, start diuretics if volume overloaded, consider vasopressors, and obtain chest X‑ray if possible.

A child with diarrhoea is dehydrated but has a serum sodium of 150 mmol/L. Which fluid is safest? — Use isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline or Ringer's lactate) to avoid worsening hypernatremia; avoid hypotonic solutions.

In a patient with septic shock, why might you add albumin after 30 ml/kg crystalloids? — Albumin can increase oncotic pressure when capillary leak persists, but only after adequate crystalloid resuscitation and if albumin is available.
How does capillary leak in severe malaria affect fluid choice? — Large volumes of isotonic crystalloids may extravasate; give smaller boluses (10‑15 ml/kg) and monitor for pulmonary oedema.

Why is 0.45% saline generally avoided in critically ill adults? — It can cause hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema, especially when ADH is high; reserve for specific cases like hypernatremic correction.
What bedside sign suggests you have given too much fluid? — Development of new peripheral oedema, rising JVP, or decreasing oxygen saturation with crackles on auscultation.
ai.title: Intravenous Fluid Therapy: Types and Uses
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A clinician must match fluid type to the patient’s volume status, electrolyte needs and underlying disease, especially in low‑resource settings where labs are limited. Understanding physiology guides safe resuscitation and maintenance.

b: Crystalloids: isotonic (0.9% saline, Ringer's lactate), hypotonic (0.45% saline), hypertonic (3% saline)
Colloids: albumin, gelatin, starches – increase oncotic pressure
sections.p: Intravenous fluids replace lost volume, correct electrolyte disturbances, and provide calories when oral intake is impossible. Choice depends on tonicity, electrolyte composition and the clinical scenario.

b: Assess volume status: capillary refill, pulse pressure, skin turgor, bedside ultrasound if available
Know the four clinical indications: resuscitation, replacement, maintenance, drug carrier
sections.p: Fluid balance follows Starling forces; isotonic crystalloids distribute quickly into the extracellular space, while colloids stay intravascular longer. In sepsis or malaria, capillary leak alters distribution.

b: Severe malaria: give isotonic crystalloid bolus 20 ml/kg, then reassess
Obstetric haemorrhage: rapid isotonic bolus 10‑20 ml/kg, consider blood if available
sections.p: In East African hospitals, common causes of hypovolemia include severe malaria, diarrhoeal disease, obstetric haemorrhage, and trauma. Limited lab access means decisions rely on bedside assessment.

t.b: Is perfusion adequate? > 3 seconds suggests hypoperfusion → give fluid bolus
Guides choice of isotonic vs. hypotonic fluid; if unavailable, use clinical clues (e.g., seizures → avoid hypotonic fluids)

b: Calculate 20 ml/kg bolus for a 60 kg adult → 1.2 L
Identify signs of fluid overload: crackles, rising JVP, decreasing urine output
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to choose, calculate, and monitor fluids, and to recognise complications such as pulmonary oedema or hypernatremia.

b: Giving hypotonic saline to a patient with hyponatraemia can worsen cerebral oedema
Continuing large crystalloids in septic shock without vasopressors may cause oedema
sections.p: Errors often stem from misunderstanding tonicity, ignoring ongoing losses, or failing to stop fluids when signs of overload appear.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling blood pressure despite 2 boluses
New onset dyspnoea with crackles after fluid administration
Severe electrolyte derangement (e.g., Na > 160 mmol/L or < 115 mmol/L) when labs become available
